611.t: Small's Paradise band and its star sidemen
611.s: He came to New York in 1926; the band at Small's Paradise had Edgar Sampson, Benny Carter, Jimmy Harrison, Jabbo Smith and Billy Taylor, and he judged Small's better than the Cotton Club for dancing girls.
611.q: Well see I came up to New York, see I came up to New York in 1926 and stayed until way into the late 40’s. And the band that I worked with see had very, very, very top musicians in it. We had Edgar Sampson, the composer of “Stomping at the Savoy,” well he was a friend of mine, see. And we had the…

611.t: Joining Charlie Johnson in Atlantic City and the 'Paradise' name
611.s: Waters headed for a big band via Philadelphia, joined Johnson in Atlantic City knowing New York was next, and claims the Paradise Ten name came from both the Atlantic City and Small's Paradise.
611.q: Well that's where I said I made a mistake of the biggest, first big band that I worked, remember I told you I made a mistake -

611.t: Had Charlie Johnson already played Small's Paradise?
611.s: Pressed by Schaap, Waters admits Elmer Snowden's band may have been at Small's before Johnson's and he cannot say the band had played New York before he joined.
611.q: I know - wait a minute, I need check on that again. They had another guitar player, guitar, banjo player that used to work with Duke Ellington, Elmer Snowden -

611.t: Resolving the Paradise name using the 1979 interview
611.s: Schaap recalls that in 1979 Waters said the name came from Atlantic City; Waters accepts it is probable that the band took its name there before reaching New York.
611.q: I think that, I think so, somethin' like that, I can't verify that so well. But I know one thing, that I knew that I was comin' to New York before I joined the band because they told me.

0.t: Cliff Jackson takes over the Nest Club band from Snowden
0.s: Snowden moved to the Bandville Club and gave his Nest Club job to Cliff Jackson, whose band Caldwell joined and named A Bunch of Keys.
0.ch: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
0.q: Snowden had a group. It was Prince Robinson (unintelligible) because they had a very good band -- at the Nest Club. So they had a club on 129th Street, just off of

0.t: Snowden, gigging and joining Charlie Johnson at Small's Paradise
0.s: After Snowden he gigged until joining Charlie Johnson's summer replacement band at Small's in 1926 while Johnson was in Atlantic City.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: Small's Paradise (unintelligible). You see, what happened, Charlie went to Atlantic City with his original band, and he asked (unintelligible) put the band in there for the summer.

91.t: Filling in the years before Charlie Johnson: Fowler and Matson
91.s: Berger asks about 1922-27; Carter recalls playing with Billy Fowler and Charlie Matson around New York.
91.q: Good. Maybe what I'm talking about is really, probably, a little later than '22, because I know that I did play with Billy Fowler, who else did I play with? I did some playing around New York with, oh, some bands who did -- Charlie Matson.

91.t: Club Bamville, Charlie Johnson and Small's Paradise
91.s: Fletcher supplied arrangements and the Collegians played Club Bamville; Carter then tried to sort out his move to Charlie Johnson at Small's Paradise and back to Horace.
91.q: Oh yes, yes. We went on the road. And then finally, we were getting some arrangements from Fletcher, his brother, Fletcher Henderson -- and then I

725.t: New Orleans Wiggle and the Piron band's New York engagements
725.s: Playing New Orleans Wiggle, he says brother Pete wrote it; recalls recording for three companies, Club Deluxe and offers from the Scandals.
725.q: He did his stuff. Pete wrote it and arranged it. And of course when it was in New York I think it was published by Williams. I'm not positive, I don't know, I'm sure it was. I know West Indies Blues was published by Clarence, you know. And uh, we did that number on uh, I think, OK recording. If I'm…

251.t: New York clubs, Jabbo Smith, and Jonah Jones from Buffalo
251.s: Questions about Charlie Johnson, the Cotton Club audition and Small's Paradise, then Jabbo Smith, Jonah Jones and the DeParis brothers.
251.ch: Records and the Don Albert band
251.q: Charlie Johnson, I can't recall the name. But I know that the Cotton Club was then on 147 in Lenox. Because we went down there for an audition when Duke was playing in there.

39.t: Keppard at the Coconut Grove with Tim Brown
39.s: Taylor describes Keppard's season with Tim Brown's big band at the Coconut Grove in New York, dated about 1919.
39.q: But Joe was most of us more of a style. And Louis still is a blue chord man. And he was a blues artist chord. And a hot chord man. But Freddie was great on breaks. He was great on... I had some kind of a new sort of... He could blue also and some of the other things he could do. Now, another thing…

43.s: Sam Wooding's orchestra and Danny Wilson's band played at the Nest, and Wooding then left for the Club Alabama and Europe.
43.q: Sam Wooding's orchestra was there. And, um, then, uh, let me see, what other people, orchestra was there? Uh, Danny Wilson, that was Edith Wilson's husband, he had a band there. And, oh, there was two, three different bands there, you know, from a minute ago. Because, uh, Sam Wooding's and left…

893.t: The Stuyvesant Casino and Bunk Johnson's band
893.s: Green describes the ballroom, the band and a brief talk with Bunk.
893.q: It was overwhelming. It was a room such as I'd never seen, this huge ballroom with the walls sort of a cream color, tables all around, a dance floor cleared in the middle, with a great crystal chandelier hanging down with—that had these little, uh, surfaces on it. And as it revolved, lights played…

571.t: Playing in bands in the 1920s, Bunk Johnson, and Sam Dutrey's father
571.s: Asked when he first played, Lewis says the late 1920s, when many bands worked around Bunk Johnson. He mentions Sam Dutrey's father.
571.q: I was here at Boghaneen before the latter part of the 20s. My favorite one. Well, I was across the lake man. Obviously here on the Appetitums. Not the Bunk's band. It wasn't Bunk's band. It was Bunker's behind. Up to Buck Canals, you had more musicians than you had down below. In the 20s, I played…

1.t: New York in the fall of 1930 and Hawkins as the wind
1.s: Barker lists the bands at the Savoy, Roseland, Smalls' Paradise and Connie's Inn and describes the cold fall winds he calls Hawkins.
1.q: So I go to New York. Now there’s Chick Webb on the Savoy. Fletcher Henderson is at Roseland. And Jelly Roll had left Rosemont. There was Charlie Johnson at Smalls’ Paradise. Fats Waller was in Connie’s Inn. Chick Webb was on the Savoy. Charlie Johnson was at Smalls’ Paradise. The city just lit up…

85.t: Charlie Johnson's orchestra at Smalls' Paradise
85.s: Carter names the Harlem bands he played with, including June Clark's sextet and Charlie Johnson at Smalls' Paradise.
85.q: Yes. Well, let’s see, who were they? Charlie Johnson, for one that had the orchestra at the Smalls’ Paradise. Prior to that I played with the sextet of June Clark, who was at Small’s smaller place. When Edwin Smalls opened his Smalls’ Paradise over on Seventh Avenue, then he put in the big band,…

26.t: Bricktop and the job at Baron Wilkins'
26.s: Bricktop gets the group a summer job at Baron Wilkins' in Harlem, where their small band sounds smoother than others.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: So that's there, he had an engagement in Chicago or somewhere, but we wouldn't go. Said no, we ain't leaving New York, so he got somebody else, so in the meantime, it's summertime now, a person called Bricktop. You heard of Bricktop.

67.t: Charlie Johnson's Paradise band and Frankie Half-Pint Jackson
67.s: He recalls Charlie Johnson's band in Atlantic City and Small's Paradise, Half-Pint Jackson the entertainer, and Johnson leaving the band to play alone.
67.q: In Atlantic City. They would work in Atlantic City in the summer and the winter they would come here, to Small's Paradise.

167.t: Washboard group at fourteen and record dates
167.s: Before Duke he played all kinds of groups, then a washboard band at the Onyx Club in New York, and was called for record dates.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: And I used to make record dates, and they'd always come for me. They wanted me to play the guitar.

381.t: Playing hotels with Billy Hicks and his Sizzler Six
381.s: He joined Billy Hicks's sextet, playing St. Regis, Astor and Waldorf rooms.
381.ch: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
381.q: So, right after that, there was a guy that had a six piece group named Billy Hicks, that was called Billy Hicks and his Sizzler Six.

124.t: With Charlie Johnson at Ed Small's club and Small's Paradise
124.s: McRae worked about a couple of months at Small's 5th Avenue club, then about a year at Small's Paradise, where he met Benny Waters and Benny Carter.
124.ch: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
124.q: It was like a private club. Then he moved me over to Small's Paradise. And I worked with Charlie Johnson there for about a year.

78.t: The Jones Beach ten-piece band and his Dunbar Palace men
78.s: He led a ten-man band at a Jones Beach club after an audition, and at the Dunbar had trumpeter Jack Butler and drummer Manzie Johnson. Tape 1 ends.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Well, there's a night club there. I've got to think of the name of this club. This is where I had a big band and we would commute. (unintelligible)
